The one place every term in the system is defined. If a document uses a word differently from this page, one of them is wrong: settle it here, then fix the document.

Core terms get two parts: **what** the thing is, and **why** we use this word for it. The why is the part to argue with. Standard industry terms are listed at the end with a single line each.

## Core terms

### Artifacts and the roadmap

**Artifact**
- **What:** Anything the team generates as part of designing, building and running a service. A roadmap, an Initiative write-up, a story map, a design file, a user story and release notes are all artifacts.
- **Why:** "Artifact" says the thing was made during the work, to be used and built on by the next step. "Record" says it was filed afterward to prove something happened. We want the first meaning.

**Artifact chain**
- **What:** The way artifacts relate to each other. Most sit in a parent-child hierarchy, the way cascading OKRs or nesting dolls do. Each one takes its purpose from the layer above and works out more detail for the layer below, so together they form one connected line of thinking from vision to user story.
- **Why:** Read upward, the chain answers "why are we doing this?" Read downward, it answers "how will this actually happen?" Gaps are signals: work with no parent has no reason to exist, and a goal with nothing beneath it isn't being pursued.

**Commitment**
- **What:** A promise the team makes at quarterly planning to deliver something specific this quarter. Each commitment has a status that updates every sprint.
- **Why:** The team controls what it delivers but not how people respond, so we hold ourselves accountable for commitments and treat goals as bets. A commitment is a promise to try. Some misses are expected, and raising them early is part of the promise.

**Deliverable**
- **What:** A tangible thing handed over: a working digital solution, a document, a training program, a guide, a discovery brief. If there is nothing to hand over, it isn't a deliverable. Learning something or talking about something doesn't count on its own.
- **Why:** The word exists so we can say, without debate, whether a commitment was met. Either the thing was delivered or it wasn't. That stops activity from passing as progress.

**Epic**
- **What:** A flexible container the team uses to group related user stories. It might follow a column on the story map, a variation such as one document type, a slice, or whatever helps the team size and organize its work. Optional. The one rule: an epic stays inside one Solution.
- **Why:** Teams need a middle-sized handle on their work, but no single shape fits every Solution, so we don't force one. The fixed chain is Solution to Deliverable to user story; an epic groups stories without being a link in that chain. It is a team tool, not a roadmap item. Older material puts a "feature" above the epic; that level is the Solution here.

**Future consideration**
- **What:** An idea log status for something we aren't doing now and haven't ruled out. The requester is told plainly: not yes, not no, and we won't follow up. If it comes up again at planning, the idea is still there.
- **Why:** Without it, the only honest answers are yes and no, and people hear silence as a quiet no or a forgotten yes. Naming the status sets the expectation once, so nobody waits on a reply that isn't coming.

**Goal**
- **What:** A change in what people do, with a starting value and a target, held for one to two years.
- **Why:** A team can deliver everything it promised and still change nothing for anyone. Writing goals as changes in behavior keeps the measure on people, not on output.

**Goal progress**
- **What:** Where each goal stands: its starting value, last and current readings, target, and a progress circle. Updated at quarterly planning.
- **Why:** It is the only part of the roadmap that reports results rather than activity. Kept apart from commitment status, it shows when the team is delivering but nothing is moving.

**Idea**
- **What:** Any suggestion, from anyone, with no commitment attached.
- **Why:** Calling it an idea lets us say yes to hearing it without saying yes to doing it. Ideas cost nothing to log, so people keep offering them.

**Idea log**
- **What:** Where ideas collect until the product manager looks across them for patterns.
- **Why:** "Log" means a record of what came in, not a list of work we owe. A backlog implies a debt to pay down in order. The idea log is a toy chest: you take out what's useful and leave the rest.

**Initiative**
- **What:** The unit of work we track: a hypothesis that pursuing an opportunity will advance a goal, held to the outcome it is meant to change. It stays open, trying one Solution after another if needed, until the outcome is reached or the bet is disproven.
- **Why:** It names taking the initiative on a problem before anyone has decided what to build, and it keeps the commitment on the outcome rather than on any one output. Its closest government equivalent is a project: a bounded effort toward one result. The difference is where it starts. A project starts from a fixed scope; an Initiative starts from an opportunity, and "don't build" is a legitimate ending.

**Intended progress**
- **What:** The team's bet for each goal this quarter: a short milestone name and what we will be able to show by quarter end, with a number.
- **Why:** Goals move slowly, and a goal at 0% can be on track or failing. Stating the bet in advance tells you which, and turns "why hasn't this moved?" into a planned conversation instead of a surprise.

**Now, Next, Later grid**
- **What:** The roadmap view of the work ahead in three time horizons, one row per goal. Now is this quarter, Next is the following two quarters, and Later is beyond that. The further out an item sits, the less concrete it is: Now holds Deliverables, Next mostly holds Solutions, and Later holds Initiatives, which are opportunities we haven't committed to solving yet.
- **Why:** Horizons instead of dates admit that we can't promise exact timing for work that far out. The items also aren't like-for-like from one column to the next. In a project plan, the milestone due in two years is the same kind of thing as the one due tomorrow. Here, a Now card is a commitment and a Later card is a question, and reading them the same way creates false promises. Janna Bastow created the time-horizon grid; making each horizon hold a different kind of artifact is Ian Swanson's addition.

**Opportunity**
- **What:** An unmet need, pain or desire, described in the words of the people who have it.
- **Why:** "Opportunity" covers desires as well as pains, and keeps the answer open: it describes what people need, not what we might build. Teresa Torres made it central to discovery. "Problem" is fine shorthand.

**Roadmap**
- **What:** The single document that holds vision and strategy, goals and goal progress, the Now, Next, Later grid, quarterly commitments and the sprint report.
- **Why:** A roadmap is not a plan, it is a guiding document that tells you where you are heading in different layers and helps you understand if you are getting to where you want to be. One document means strategy and status are read together. Split across files, they drift apart, and nobody can see whether this sprint's work still serves this year's goals.

**Release notes**
- **What:** Messages that tell staff, partners and the public what changed, written for the person whose experience changes.
- **Why:** Shipping something nobody hears about delivers nothing. Release notes close the loop with the people who asked, including the person whose idea started the work.

**Roadmap item**
- **What:** Any card on the Now, Next, Later grid: an Initiative, a Solution or a Deliverable.
- **Why:** It gives us one word for "something on the roadmap" without pretending the three types of work are the same thing.

**Digital solution**
- **What:** Any digital means of solving a problem: configuring a tool we already have (a Microsoft Form, a SharePoint list), adopting a product, automating a step, or building custom software.
- **Why:** A typical software development lifecycle is designed to produce custom-built software. Digital government shares its disciplines (discovery, slicing, release, enable) but not that assumption. Calling the output a digital solution keeps the cheaper, faster options on the table: sometimes a Microsoft Form solves the problem, and building bespoke software would be the wrong move.

**Solution**
- **What:** One way the team tries to reach an Initiative's outcome: an output that gets tested, built, kept or dropped. It can be a digital solution, content, a process change or training. An Initiative may try several.
- **Why:** The word says nothing about form, so the team doesn't default to building software, and it is named for the problem it solves. Keeping Solutions beneath the Initiative means a Solution that doesn't move the outcome can be dropped without dropping the goal.

**Sprint report**
- **What:** The part of the roadmap updated every sprint: whether the sprint goal was met, where each commitment stands, and what is blocked.
- **Why:** Two weeks is the shortest loop at which the team can change course. Reporting at that rhythm means a slip shows up while there is still time to recover.

**User story**
- **What:** The smallest piece of value the team builds, described from the user's side: As a [user], I need to [action], so that I can [benefit].
- **Why:** A story is a placeholder for a conversation, not a specification. Writing it from the user's side keeps the reason in view. "Need" rather than "want" asks whether the thing is necessary, not just preferred.

### Strategy

**Outcome**
- **What:** What changes for people because of the work. An output is what the team ships.
- **Why:** Outputs are easier to count, so they take over unless outcomes are named. The distinction keeps "we built what you asked for" from standing in for "we achieved what you need."

**Service**
- **What:** Something that helps someone do something (Lou Downe's definition), and that people rely on over time, with no finish line and needs that keep changing.
- **Why:** Its closest government equivalent is a program. We say "service" for two reasons. IT service management already treats technology as services delivered to the people who use them, so the word connects to how IT runs. And service design grounds it in the person's experience, not the organization's structure: a resident renews a registration; they don't interact with a division.

**Strategy**
- **What:** How we intend to reach the vision: a diagnosis of what is wrong, a guiding approach, three to five key actions and the tradeoffs we accept.
- **Why:** A strategy is a set of choices, including what we won't do. Without those choices it is a wish list, and every request looks equally worth doing.

**Vision**
- **What:** The future the service creates for people, written to last five years or more.
- **Why:** It is meant to outlast a change of leadership, so it describes what people experience, not what we build. It is the fixed point everything else in the artifact chain traces back to.

### Planning and status

**Capacity**
- **What:** The working days the team has in a quarter, after holidays and organization business, split across the three work types. The split is set each quarter at planning.
- **Why:** Commitments only mean something against a known amount of time. Counting capacity first is what makes a commitment honest.

**Delivery type**
- **What:** How a Deliverable lands: released to users, put in service behind the scenes, or handed off to another team or to staff.
- **Why:** "Done" means different things for a digital solution, infrastructure and training. Naming the delivery type up front makes it clear what counts as delivered.

**Ongoing commitment**
- **What:** A standing service level for continuous work, such as "security patches within 48 hours" or "2-week average response time on small requests."
- **Why:** Continuous work is never done, so it can't be committed to as a Deliverable. A service level is the only promise about it we can check.

**Required**
- **What:** A tag for work mandated by law, policy or compliance. Required work may have no Initiative: it traces to its mandate instead.
- **Why:** A mandate says the work must happen. It doesn't say what type of work it is or how sure we are. As a tag, required work stays visible and still competes for capacity, instead of hiding in a column of its own.

**Small request**
- **What:** A bounded change to something that already exists, finished in less than a sprint, that doesn't advance a roadmap goal.
- **Why:** These requests need a quick, predictable answer, not a debate about priorities. Separating them protects requesters from waiting on the roadmap, and protects the roadmap from being nibbled away.

**Status labels**
- **What:** Committed, On track, Off track and Done. Used for commitments only.
- **Why:** There is deliberately no "at risk." A middle label lets bad news wait. With only Off track, a slip is either fine or needs a recovery plan now.

**Strategic**
- **What:** The work type that advances a roadmap goal, through discovery or delivery. 
- **Why:** Naming it gives goal work a protected share, so it doesn't get squeezed out by whatever is loudest this week.

**T-shirt size**
- **What:** A rough measure of how much focused work an item takes for the people doing it, counted in two-week sprints. XS is a few hours, S is a sprint or less, M is about 2 sprints, L is 3 to 4 sprints, XL is 5 or more. A Solution can be XL; a Deliverable can't.
- **Why:** The sizes are coarse on purpose: they signal how uncertain the work still is. Sprints are a unit stakeholders can picture. Measuring focused work, not time on the calendar, keeps waiting and approvals on the schedule where they belong.

**Technical maintenance**
- **What:** The work type that keeps services running, healthy and secure, and keeps the team working well. 25% of capacity by default.
- **Why:** "Operational work" reads as a separate track and becomes a dumping ground. Technical maintenance names the purpose, keeping what we've built healthy, and treats it as part of running the service.

**Work types**
- **What:** The three kinds of work every quarter is split across: Strategic, Technical maintenance and Small requests. The default is 50/25/25. The split is decided each quarter at planning, based on the work at hand, and changes for longer stretches when something systemic calls for it, such as a legacy system near end of life or a team that mostly runs services.
- **Why:** Without a protected share, one kind of work always wins. Usually it's the roadmap, and maintenance and requests quietly rot. Naming the three types makes all of the work visible and keeps the balance deliberate. Setting the split each quarter, and saying why it moved from the default, keeps it honest rather than habitual.

### Process

**Champion**
- **What:** A partner staff member who learns a service early, helps peers, and reports back what they hear.
- **Why:** The team can't be in every office. Champions spread know-how and bring back what's really happening. They advocate; the product manager decides.

**Discovery**
- **What:** The learning work inside an Initiative: finding which problems are worth solving and which Solutions would work. Each round is timeboxed and ends in a decision about a Solution: build it, don't build it, or try something different.
- **Why:** It is not requirements gathering. Requirements gathering assumes we will build something. Discovery can conclude that we shouldn't, and that is a successful result.

**Enable**
- **What:** The step that makes sure people can succeed with what was released: guides, training and champions, alternating with listening and feedback. It starts while the team is still building.
- **Why:** A service that ships but isn't used delivers nothing. Making Enable a named step puts training and feedback in the plan, with capacity, instead of leaving them to whoever has time after launch.

**Launch**
- **What:** The moment people outside the team are expected to start using something new.
- **Why:** See Release. The two words separate getting a digital solution into production from getting people ready for it.

**Release**
- **What:** Putting working digital solutions into production, even if it is switched off or visible only to a beta group.
- **Why:** Separating release from launch lets the team ship small and often, while each launch waits until the people affected are ready. Technical risk and organizational readiness get handled separately.

**Triage**
- **What:** A weekly review that gives every incoming request a destination and gives every requester an answer.
- **Why:** The word comes from emergency medicine: sort quickly by what each case needs, rather than fixing each one as it arrives. The promise is a fast answer, not a yes.

## Standard terms

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| Acceptance criteria | The conditions a story must meet to be accepted, written as Given / When / Then scenarios. |
| Advisory group | Partners and community voices who meet monthly to check strategic fit and hear where the work and goals stand. They advise and don't move items. |
| Assumption | Something that must be true for a solution to work. Four types: desirable, viable, feasible, usable. |
| Backlog | The ordered stories under each Deliverable, owned by the product owner. |
| Concierge test | People do by hand what the software would do later, to test an idea before building it. |
| Content strategist | Leads Enable, brings editors' and partners' requests to triage, and joins work that changes words people read. |
| Definition of done | The checklist every story must meet to count as finished, including being deployable. |
| Definition of ready | The checklist a story must meet before it enters a sprint. |
| Development team | The people who build, test and release, and who estimate and commit to stories. |
| Diagnosis | The part of the strategy that says what is wrong today and why. |
| Direction review | The yearly meeting that checks vision, strategy and goals, ahead of budget requests. |
| Discovery brief | The one-page summary of a discovery effort: timebox, team, riskiest assumptions and the decision. |
| Executive steering group | Leaders who own the vision and strategy, set goals with the product manager, approve resources to pursue large Initiatives, and meet monthly to hear status and settle escalations. |
| Fit check | At planning, comparing the sizes each person owns with their Strategic sprints. |
| Focus areas | Where the strategy chooses to concentrate. |
| Functional manager | The person someone reports to on the organization chart. Owns performance, career and time off, not the order of the work. |
| Guiding approach | Guiding principles plus focus areas: how we choose between competing work. |
| Guiding principles | The rules we use when two good options compete. |
| Hand off | A delivery type: the Deliverable passes to another team or to staff. |
| In service | A delivery type: a system or shared component goes into production use behind the scenes. |
| INVEST | The test for a good story: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. |
| Key actions | Three to five big moves in the strategy, each strengthening the others. |
| Learning slice | A slice that tests the riskiest remaining assumption with real users. |
| Listening session | A one-on-one conversation where someone walks through the last time they did the thing. |
| Opportunity solution tree | Outcome, then opportunities, then solutions, then tests, used to compare at least three solutions per opportunity. |
| Process flow | The eight steps: capture ideas, set direction, plan the quarter, discover, slice the work, build and release, review the sprint, enable. |
| Product manager | Owns the roadmap, the idea log, Initiatives and Solutions, and makes the final call on priorities. |
| Product owner | Owns the small request board and the backlog, runs triage, writes stories and accepts finished work. |
| Product trio | A product manager, a designer and an engineer running discovery together. |
| Progress circle | Grey, green, yellow or red on goal progress, judged against intended progress. |
| Quarter review | The meeting on the last day of the quarter that marks each commitment Done or rolled forward. |
| Quarterly planning | Four half-day sessions before the quarter: candidates, sizing, technical maintenance and capacity, commitment. |
| Readiness check | Before a launch, asking each affected group whether it is ready. No reply counts as yes. |
| Refinement | The meeting where Deliverables are sliced into stories that meet the definition of ready. |
| Release slice | A thin, usable path across the story map that can ship as one release. |
| Retro | The end-of-sprint meeting where the team reflects on how it works and picks changes to try. |
| Scrum master | Runs the sprint meetings, keeps the sprint numbers, and guards the definitions of ready and done. |
| Small request board | The product owner's queue of small requests, worked first in, first out. Urgency or the product owner can change the order. |
| Spike | A short, timeboxed investigation that answers one question so a story can be estimated. |
| Sprint | A two-week cycle of planning, building, review and retro. Six to a quarter. |
| Sprint goal | The one-sentence aim a sprint is planned around. |
| Sprint planning | The meeting that sets the sprint goal and the stories committed. |
| Sprint review | The meeting that demos the work and updates the sprint report. |
| Story map | The user's steps left to right, stories underneath, sliced into releases. |
| Story points | An optional team estimate for stories: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Split at 8, must split at 13. |
| Technical architect | Checks feasibility, names technical dependencies and leads the Technical maintenance list. |
| Tradeoffs | What the strategy says we will not do, defer or ignore. |
| UX designer and researcher | Plans and runs discovery research and owns design readiness. |
| Value stream | Who a service ultimately serves: community, staff or enabling. |
| Vertical slice | Work through every layer so a user can do something new. |

## Words we avoid

| Avoid | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| At risk | Off track | A middle label lets bad news wait. |
| Capability | Solution, or Deliverable | Too vague to check: is a better training guide a capability? |
| Feature | Solution, or Deliverable | Assumes the answer is software when it may be content, process or training. In older material, a feature is a Solution. |
| Operational work | Technical maintenance | Reads as a separate track and becomes a dumping ground. |
| Records | Artifacts | Records are filed. Artifacts are built on. |

Contrasts are fine: "outcomes, not features shipped" uses the word to name what we move away from. Older material banned "Initiative" and "Opportunity"; that ban is lifted.

## Government equivalents

| Government term | Closest term here | The difference |
|---|---|---|
| Program | Service | A program is organized around funding and structure; a service is organized around what it helps someone do. |
| Project | Initiative | A project starts from a fixed scope; an Initiative starts from an opportunity and can end in "don't build." |
